claims: Flea-borne (murine) typhus is a bacterial disease.
Flea-borne typhus is caused by Rickettsia typhi or Rickettsia felis.
Flea-borne typhus is transmitted to humans via infected flea feces.
Infected flea feces are often from cats, rats, or opossums.
Symptoms of flea-borne typhus typically appear 6–14 days after exposure to infected flea feces.
Infected flea feces can enter the body through cuts, scrapes, or being rubbed into the eyes.
The cat flea (Ctenocephalides felis) is the primary carrier in the United States.
Infected fleas defecate while biting a human.
The bacteria enters the bloodstream when the person scratches the bite area.
Flea-borne typhus can also be transmitted by breathing in dust containing dried flea feces.
Fleas often live on cats, rats, opossums, raccoons, skunks, and rodents.
High fever is a common symptom of flea-borne typhus.
Headache is a common symptom of flea-borne typhus.
Chills are a common symptom of flea-borne typhus.
Body aches and muscle pain are common symptoms of flea-borne typhus.
Nausea and vomiting are common symptoms of flea-borne typhus.
Rash is a common symptom of flea-borne typhus.
Rash starts several days after initial symptoms.
Cough is a common symptom of flea-borne typhus.
Most cases of flea-borne typhus are mild.
Some patients can develop severe illness, including meningitis or organ damage.
Deaths are rare (less than 1% of cases).
Cases are often severe enough to require hospitalization.
Prompt treatment with antibiotics (specifically doxycycline) is effective.
Doctors often use blood tests (serology) and base diagnosis on clinical symptoms, especially if the patient is in a high-risk area.
Flea-borne typhus is found worldwide, especially in tropical and subtropical climates.
In the United States, flea-borne typhus is most common in Southern California, Hawaii, and Texas.
